answers.text: In short, one instruction: return exactly three lines, in order -- delivery date, item and quantity, change from original order -- using a fixed template. Label each line (Date / Item & Qty / Change) so it's unambiguous which line is which. If no change is mentioned, the template still outputs 'Change: none noted' rather than dropping the line. It's the fixed template, not the wording of the summary, that forces the same three lines every run.

Bottom line: structure: submitter, date range, itemised lines (date, amount, category), total -- in that fixed order. The total is the sum of the amount column, stated once at the end, not estimated. Identical-looking lines (same date, amount, category) are kept as separate claims, not merged.

There's an error in this email. The call was on the 14th; the 19th is five days later, not the 'three days out' the email states. The delivery date and the 'three days out' line can't both be right. I'd check today's actual date and the call notes against the calendar before it's sent.

Straightforwardly, the 15% delivery growth (54 to 62) checks out fine. The on-time rate is wrong: 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%. Stock 'held steady' at 340 despite a 15% jump in deliveries -- that's unexplained. I'd pull the actual late-delivery count and depot stock levels from source records, not just re-check the report's own arithmetic.

I'd sign off Output 2 -- it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 gives no way to see the €612,000 or €25,100 it's built from. The 4.1% could well be right, but there's no way to know without re-running it. Even with Output 2, I'd still check the €612,000 and €25,100 against the Q2 ledger.

In short, I'd send Reply 2 -- it names the order and credit references. Reply 1 claims 'entirely our error' and a credit with no order number or reference to check it against. That doesn't make Reply 1 wrong -- once checked, it could still go out as written. Before sending Reply 1, I'd confirm the order and the credit note actually posted.

Bottom line: 1. No -- that's the customer's delivery address, personal data tied to an identifiable customer. 3. No -- next quarter's pricing is unreleased and competitively sensitive. 4. Yes -- it's already published on our own site, so nothing new is exposed. 2. Yes, it's an aggregate sales figure with no customer detail. 5. No, that's a colleague's personal mobile number -- personal data too.

Unit pricing and volume discounts are sensitive -- redact the figures before pasting anything in. The confidentiality clause names both companies, which makes it a harder no than a generic clause would be. The delivery schedule on its own is low-risk and fine to paste as-is. For the pricing and the clause, I'd paraphrase without figures or names, or use a vetted tool instead.

Straightforwardly, I'd cross-cast the report's totals against the delivery log itself every week. That happens Friday, right before the report goes to the ops manager. Recomputing from the log catches a wrong total or a fabricated line, not just a typo. I own that check, and if it fails the report goes back for a redraft, not out the door.

Step 1 -- extracting the item list and quantities -- is where an error would compound downstream. But step 4, the automatic send, is where it becomes irreversible -- that's where the gate belongs. It should flag any extracted quantity above a set threshold, or stock availability that's borderline rather than clear-cut. If it trips, nothing sends automatically -- it routes to whoever's on order-processing that day.
